title: The Hidden Costs of Green Trade: Environmental Regulation, Market Access, and Unequal Value Capture in West African Cocoa Supply Chains
content: The study investigates hidden costs of green trade, focusing on environmental regulation, market access, and unequal value capture in West African cocoa supply chains. Environmental due diligence increases the commercial importance of verified origin information, reshaping supplier relationships and the distribution of compliance burdens. Focusing on Côte d’Ivoire, with Ghana and five additional West African producers providing regional context, the analysis combines 2016–2024 cocoa export destinations with 2024 trader-level procurement disclosures. An exposure–visibility decomposition measures European market dependence and public sourcing traceability, while sharp allocation bounds and an aggregate adding-up constraint examine indirect procurement among six major trading groups. In 2024, 66.16% of Ivorian cocoa exports were directed to the European Union, and EU-bound indirect sourcing together with undisclosed-origin trade represented 31.70% of national exports. Despite incomplete company-level cross-tabulations, eight pairwise comparisons identify guaranteed differences in EU-bound indirect procurement volumes. A disclosure-priority measure identifies where additional transaction information could reduce uncertainty effectively. The study advances the literature by connecting identifiable trade-network structures to the economic governance of traceability and by specifying how disclosure requirements can address consequential information gaps. A complementary framework examines producer adaptation costs, buyer screening, record portability, and bargaining opportunities as channels shaping inclusive market participation and value capture. Policy implications concern targeted data disclosure, interoperable verification systems, and safeguards for supplier mobility. The trade-based evidence identifies sourcing exposure and asymmetries in public disclosure; producer-level distributional outcomes and environmental effects require linked farm, buyer, and ecological records. Across countries, institutional differences warrant cautious interpretation of regional comparisons.
